newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE's big show raises arms makers' hopes.
newsitem.headline: UAE's big show raises arms makers' hopes.

text.p: Abu Dhabi, a quiet desert capital, will turn into a frenzy of arms salesmen trying to cash in on a growing Gulf Arab appetite for military hardware when the Middle East's biggest arms show opens on Sunday.
Some 700 international companies are flocking to the United Arab Emirates' capital to promote everything from underwater weapons to tanks to optic systems.
Many at the show will be asking the $6 billion question -- will the UAE announce a long-awaited deal for up to 80 fighters?

For months markets have been rife with talk that Abu Dhabi could award the contract to one or both of the remaining bidders -- France's Dassault Aviation and Lockheed Martin Corp of the United States -- at the five-day International Defence Exhibition and Conference (IDEX).
The package, potentially worth $6 billion, could be the world's last arms contract of its size this century.

France is riding on hopes that its intense lobbying and history of lucrative deals in the oil-rich emirate will help it clinch the deal. Abu Dhabi has already purchased tanks and planes including helicopters from Paris.
The United States has been banking on cashing in political credit earned in the 1991 Gulf War to steer most or all of the package to Lockheed Martin.
The Bethesda, Maryland-based firm has begun its IDEX lobbying with full-page advertisements in local newspapers featuring its F-16 Fighting Falcon soaring skywards.
Industry sources say the UAE could divide the package between Dassault and Lockheed to protect political interests and diversify its suppliers.
"They always try to reduce vulnerability and they don't want to depend on one supplier and one country," one source said.
Other deals that might be announced at IDEX include a contract potentially worth $1 billion to supply Abu Dhabi with up to six fast patrol boats, industry sources say.

Raytheon and Russia's Antei will also be keeping their ears open for any sign that Abu Dhabi is finally going to award a $500 million to $1 billion deal for an air defence missile system after six years of deliberations.

Many industry executives will be seeking access to the man with the key to big contracts -- Sheikh Mohammad bin Zaid al-Nahayan, UAE armed forces chief of staff and the country's leading arms procurement officer.
He has said the UAE would announce several deals at IDEX.
"Executives will be trying to speak to Sheikh Mohammad right up until the last minute before deals are announced," said one executive.

IDEX focuses the spotlight on Abu Dhabi, richest of the seven emirates which make up the UAE. It is blessed with political stability but is deeply suspicious of regional powerhouse Iran which is locked in a territorial dispute with the UAE over a group of Gulf islands.
Abu Dhabi spent about $6 billion on military hardware in the 1987-94 period.
IDEX exhibitors range from such names as Britain's Avon Inflatables to the Russian Federal Nuclear Centre to big market players like General Dynamics and Sikorsky.

While there are many defence hopefuls who will display their wares and compete for deals, industry players agree on one thing -- contracts do not come easy in Abu Dhabi and assuming you have won can be as dangerous as the weapons you are promoting.

"The Americans were just about to celebrate, but at the last minute, the French won the tank deal," said one industry executive, referring to a $3.62 billion package French arms maker Giat Industries won in 1993 to supply the UAE with 463 Leclerc battle tanks.
"You cannot afford to be too confident," he added.
